title: Sukhmani close
hookLine: a psalm for peace in any week

lines: ONE STONE FROM A LONG TRIP.
cards: Some people keep one thing from a long trip. Not the whole suitcase of souvenirs; one thing. A smooth stone from a beach, a ticket stub, a recipe written on a napkin.

Years later, holding it, the whole trip comes back: the light, the smells, who you were then. One small thing carries the rest. We've spent a hundred days walking through Sukhmani, from remembering to peace.
At the close, the question is simple. What will you keep?

teach.h: A PSALM FOR EVERY KIND OF WEEK.
teach.b: Sukhmani has been called a psalm of peace, and Sikhs turn to it in every kind of week: in a hospital waiting room, before an exam, at a new baby's welcome, on the anniversary of a death, and on ordinary Tuesdays when nothing in particular is wrong.
That range is the point. Its peace isn't only for good weeks or only for bad ones.

teach.h: WHAT WE WALKED, FROM SIMRAN TO PEACE.
teach.b: Look back at what we walked. Simran: remembering, and finding peace. The God-conscious person, humble as the earth.
Honest pages on pride and slander and clever schemes. Wealth that stays behind, and kindness that travels. A wanderer at the door, a beggar asking for mercy.

The stillness before creation, the Lord of every living thing, the eye-ointment of wisdom, the perfect One. And at the center, the line the whole bani grows from: the jewel of peace is the ambrosial Name.
Nobody holds all of that at once. That's why today's practice is to keep one piece.

teach.h: KEEP ONE PIECE, LIKE A STONE.
teach.b: Many Sikhs have a favorite stanza they know by heart and return to when they need it, like the stone from the beach: one piece that brings the whole back.
Tomorrow we move to a new bani, Asa di Var, the ballad sung at dawn in gurdwaras, by Guru Nanak, with saloks by Guru Nanak and Guru Angad.
It's a very different sound: bolder, sharper, written to a folk tune. But Sukhmani doesn't end because we've moved on. It's a circle, and whatever you keep from it, you can return to in any week.

how: Sikhs recite Sukhmani Sahib in every kind of week, in hard times, at milestones and on ordinary days, and many keep a favorite stanza by heart to return to.

o: peace and ease of the mind
a deep sleep without any dreams

p: the next bani: a ballad at dawn
like a stone from a long trip

s: Sukhmani is recited only in times of trouble
Sikhs turn to it in every kind of week, ordinary ones too.
many Sikhs keep a favorite Sukhmani stanza by heart
one piece that brings the whole back.
Asa di Var, the next bani, is also by Guru Arjan
it's Guru Nanak's var, with saloks by Guru Nanak and Guru Angad.

games.q: a hundred days of Sukhmani are ending. you can't hold it all. what does today's practice suggest?
o: try to memorize all twenty-four ashtpadis tonight.
keep one ashtpadi or picture, and return to it.
games.why: keep one piece. like a stone from a long trip, it carries the rest, and Sukhmani's circle is there to return to in any week.

practice: Let the last hundred days drift past: the beggar at the door, the stillness before creation, the eye-ointment, the earth that bears everything, the kindness that travels.
Don't choose by thinking; notice which picture your mind keeps returning to, and hold it gently, like a stone in your palm. If you pray, rest in Waheguru with it.

wordCard.voice: Sukh, peace or ease: a psalm of peace for any week, we close our hundred days by keeping one piece of it, to bring the whole back when needed.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: sukh, peace or ease, the first half of Sukhmani's name.

carryVoice: Your line: peace, kept. Thank you for walking all hundred of these days with me.
